messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken and D-RUG,

Thank you for sending and fixing your approach. I think that it does the trick, but I haven't put it through the ringer test-wise.

For those interested, I opted to use Jaime's solution (see below) as I got it working first under the scenarios that I tested. I also worked on a version of the rle() approach working that Noam and Vince offered, but I recall that I had some issues getting it to work (both runs above and below the threshold value are tallied). I've included a quick example using functions for each approach, including my original version.

Sorry that I took a few weeks to report back to the group and many thanks to D-RUG for the help.

Thank you all -
Patrick

----------------------------------
# Here's an example using
set.seed(1)
runl <- 4
value <- 100
z <- rnorm(50, value, 10)

# The candidate functions
# Ken's solution
kenf(x=z, value = value, runl = runl)
# Jaime's solution
JA_consec(z, value = value, run_length = runl)
# The rle() approach from Noam and Vince [I wasn't able to catch all errors when I tested it]
vec_QE_count(z, run_length = runl, value = value)
# Patrick's original function
QE_counter(data = data.frame(z=z), value, runl)

# The functions:

# Ken's solution

kenf <- function(x, value = 100, runl = 4) {
  y <- which(x <  value)
  ans <- min(y[runl:length(y)][ y[runl:length(y)] - y[ 1:(length(y) -(runl-1)) ] == (runl -1)])
  return(ans)
}

kenf(x=z, value = value, runl = runl)

# Jaime's function
JA_consec <- function(z, value, run_length) {

  i.low <- which(z < value)

  i.last <- i.low[1]

  counter <- 1
  for( i in i.low[-1]){

    if(counter == run_length)  return(as.integer(i.last)) #  need the double to ensure that data.table gets what it expects

    if(i-1 == i.last)  counter <- counter + 1 else counter <- 1

    if(i == i.low[length(i.low)] & counter < run_length) i.last <- NA else i.last <- i
  }
  if (is.null(class(i.last))) print("error here")
  return(as.integer(i.last))
}

# rle approach Noam and Vince
# didn't get to work quite right

vec_QE_count <- function(z, run_length, value) {
  rl <- rle(z <= value)
  if (max(rl$length[which(rl$values == 1)]) >= run_length ) {
    OUT <- sum(rl$length[1:(min(which(rl$length >= run_length & rl$values == 1))-1) ] ) + run_length
  } else {
    OUT <- NA # if no runs are at least 4
  }
  return(OUT)
}

vec_QE_count(z, run_length = runl, value = value)

# Finally, my original approach
QE_counter <- function(data, value, runl) {

  extInd <- vector("integer", ncol(data))
  for (h in 1:ncol(data)) {
    qeInd <- which(data[,h] <= value)
    extRuns <- vector("integer", 0)
    k <- 1
    if (length(qeInd) >= runl) {
      for (i in 1:(length(qeInd)-3)) {
        if (qeInd[i] == (qeInd[i+1] - 1) & qeInd[i] == (qeInd[i+2] - 2) &
              qeInd[i] == (qeInd[i+3] - 3)  ) {
          extRuns[k] <- (qeInd[i] + 3)
          k <- k + 1
        }
      }
    } else {
      extRuns[k] <- (nrow(data) + 1)
      k <- k+1
    }
    if(length(extRuns > 0)) extInd[h] <- min(extRuns) else extInd[h] <- NA
  }
  return(extInd)
} # end QE_count

Hi, Bonnie.  I don't know that  there's any harm in using a loop, although using a loop does seem to lose you some style points in the R community.

One approach to avoiding the explicit use of a loop would be to name the columns of your data frame and name your functions with the same names.  Then you could iterate over the names, as per the appended code, which applies the function "sum" to the first column of a data frame and the function "mean" to the second column.  (Note that the formatting may have suffered in the transition to email.)

-- Mike

myFns <- list(odds=sum, evens=mean)
myDF <- data.frame(
      cbind(
          odds=c(1, 3, 5, 7),
          evens=c(2, 4, 6, 8)
      )
   )

myDF

result <- lapply(names(myFns), function(nextName) {
      myFns[[nextName]](myDF[[nextName]])
})

unlist(result)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bonnie,
Some more specifics would be helpful, but if I can recommend a few packages that I use frequently for date-time conversions, 'lubridate', and 'xts'. Depending on what you are doing, POSIXct is generally the easiest and most versatile, but POSIXlt has it's uses as well.  If you simply converting a datetime, lubridate is quite easy to use:

## Some times
time1<- c("5/8/2013 08:19 PM")
time2<-c("2013-10-08 20:12:11")
time3<-c("8/6/12")
time4<-c("3.4.2012")

## See data type:
str(time1)
    chr "5/8/2013 08:19 PM"

## Convert to POSIXct
time1<-mdy_hm(time1)
str(time1)
    POSIXct[1:1], format: "2013-05-08 20:19:00"

time2<-ymd_hms(time2)
time3<-mdy(time3)
time4<-mdy(time4)

You can also pull out years, months, year-days, etc. with lubridate very easily once in POSIXct.
time2mon<-month(time2)
time2year<-year(time2)
etc...

Or round dates and times as needed with floor_date, round_date, and ceiling_date commands. See http://www.inside-r.org/node/65031.

Hope this helps, and if you have something more specific feel free to let me know.

Ryan

Thanks Ryan and Michael for the replies.  Here are some more details about my data and a couple of specific questions.

I am working with a data set of sleep records, collected from people via the internet.  Nine of the variables in this data set are time/date variables.  Eight of these variables are time and date stamps when an event occurred, such as going to bed, the alarm going off in the morning, or getting up.  One of the most important calculations I will need to do is to calculate time in bed for each night of sleep (the amount of time elapsed between going to bed and getting up).  The other time/date variable is the person's answer to the question, "What time do you have to wake up on weekdays/workdays in order to start your day successfully?", with answers rounded to the nearest 15 minutes, such as, 07:30, 08:15, 06:00, etc.

Right now I am cleaning this data set and preparing it for analysis, so I need to make decisions about which data class to use for each variable.  Ideally, I would like the simplicity of using the same time/date class for all of these nine variables.

Here are some specific questions I have about the time/date class options:
1)  That last variable (the time when the person usually needs to get up) would be best stored as just a time without any associated date.  Is there a way of doing this in the POSIX classes?  At present the only option for this that I am aware of is in the chron package:

> require(chron)
Loading required package: chron
> times("12:37:09")
[1] 12:37:09

(It would be most ideal if there were a way of storing just hours and minutes for this variable, since adding a couple of zeros for the seconds will give the data a false sense of precision, but I am not currently aware of any way to do that.)

2)  For calculating time in bed, it's my understanding that a POSIX class would have greater accuracy than chron by accounting for daylight savings time transitions.  But I would need to determine each person's time zone based on the state and zip code info they provided.  (It seems that this would be neither easy nor totally accurate, so I will need to decide whether it is worth doing for the sake of the two nights of the year with DST transitions.)  Here is what I am not clear on:  Do the POSIX classes have a way of distinguishing local time zone variations?  For example, is there a way of specifying Arizona differently from the rest of the mountain time zone (since Arizona does not observe DST in the summer like the rest of mountain time does)?  I hoping that POSIX could figure out whether DST was in effect based on the date if given the person's location specified in the right way.

Currently I am considering just using chron for all my time/date variables for the sake of simplicity, and excluding the two dates each year with DST transitions from the analysis.  But I would welcome any suggestions that anyone has for how best to handle these variables.

Thank you very much for any info or ideas.

Bonnie

A few quick notes...you can still use POSIXct (and lubridate) and then simply pull out the times of interest. I think overall working with POSIXct will be easiest for analysis and plotting in the long run (ggplot works best too). If you are only getting times in your data/response, you can always simply paste in an arbitrary date, round/snap to the nearest 15 minutes (see function below), and then pull just hour and minute out (or use decimal hours) as a new vector.

## Paste an arbitrary date and save as POSIXct:
dat <- data.frame(night.time = c("09:23:00","12:04:00", "11:03:00"))
dat$time <- as.POSIXct(paste("2013-08-01", dat$night.time)))

## Create decimal hours using lubridate...useful for statistical analysis
hrmin <- hour(dat$time) + minute(dat$time)/60

And finally...a short line to round times to nearest 15 minutes (but you can change it to whatever you'd like)
require(lubridate)
minute(dat$time)<-minute(dat$time) %/% 15 * 15

AIC (or AICc for small sample sizes) is fast becoming the standard way to compare complex models. AIC deals with the trade-off between the goodness of the model and the complexity of the model. You want to choose the model that minimizes AIC. What package are you using for gams? mgcv doesn't automatically give you AIC values, but you can get them with the function conveniently called AIC. You can also use the AICtab function in the bbmle package to produce a table comparing your models.

library("bbmle")
AICtab(model1, model2,  base = TRUE, weights = TRUE, nobs=nrow(dataset))

Hope that helps.
Rosemary
